We study theoretically the properties of two Bose-Einstein condensates in different spin states, represented by a double Fock state. Individual measurements of the spins of the particles are performed in transverse directions, giving access to the relative phase of the condensates. Initially, this phase is completely undefined, and the first measurements provide random results. But a fixed value of this phase rapidly emerges under the effect of the successive quantum measurements, giving rise to a quasi-classical situation where all spins have parallel transverse orientations. If the number of measurements reaches its maximum (the number of particles), quantum effects show up again, giving rise to violations of Bell type inequalities. The violation of BCHSH inequalities with an arbitrarily large number of spins may be comparable (or even equal) to that obtained with two spins.

# Emergence of Relative Phase and Quantum Correlations in Double Fock State Condensates

## Theoretical Framework

We present a theoretical study of a system consisting of two Bose-Einstein condensates prepared in distinct spin states. This composite system is naturally modeled as a double Fock state—a quantum many-body state characterized by a fixed, well-defined number of particles in each of the two spin components, while the relative phase between the condensates remains, at the outset, completely unspecified. This lack of initial phase definition is a hallmark of Fock states and stands in contrast to coherent-state descriptions where the phase is assumed from the start.

## Accessing the Relative Phase via Spin Measurements

To probe the relative phase between the two condensates, we consider individual spin measurements performed along transverse directions (i.e., directions orthogonal to the axis defining the two original spin states). Such transverse measurements are sensitive precisely to the coherence and relative phase information between the two Fock components, since projections along the quantization axis alone would only reveal population imbalances, not phase information.

## Dynamical Emergence of a Definite Phase

A central result of our analysis concerns the dynamical behavior of the relative phase under repeated measurement. Because the initial double Fock state contains no intrinsic phase information, the very first spin measurements yield essentially random outcomes—reflecting the complete phase uncertainty of the initial state. However, as successive measurements are performed on the ensemble of atoms, a striking phenomenon occurs: a specific, fixed value of the relative phase rapidly emerges and stabilizes. This build-up of phase coherence is a genuinely quantum measurement-induced effect, arising from the progressive collapse of the total quantum state as information about the relative phase is extracted measurement by measurement.

## Emergence of Quasi-Classical Behavior

As this phase value crystallizes, the system evolves toward a quasi-classical regime. In this regime, the individual atomic spins effectively align along a common transverse direction determined by the emergent phase, mimicking the behavior expected of a classical system with a well-defined, shared orientation. This alignment represents an effective symmetry breaking of the initial phase invariance, induced entirely by the measurement process itself rather than by any external field or interaction.

## Re-emergence of Quantum Correlations at the Full Measurement Limit

Perhaps the most striking feature of this measurement-induced dynamics appears when the number of individual spin measurements approaches the total number of particles in the system. In this regime, quantum effects—seemingly suppressed during the intermediate quasi-classical phase—make a dramatic reappearance. Specifically, we find that the correlations between measurement outcomes can violate Bell-type inequalities of the Clauser-Horne-Shimony-Holt (CHSH) form. Remarkably, the degree of violation achieved in this many-body, many-measurement regime can be comparable to, and in certain cases even reach the same magnitude as, the maximal violations obtained in the canonical two-spin (EPR-type) scenario. This result demonstrates that genuine quantum nonlocality, far from being washed out by the accumulation of measurements and the emergence of classical-like phase coherence, can survive and manifest itself at the level of the full many-particle system.

# Emergence and Fragility of Relative Phase in a Double Fock State: A Transverse Spin Measurement Approach

## Introduction

The question of how relative phase coherence emerges between two initially phase-uncertain Bose-Einstein condensates has occupied a central place in the study of quantum measurement and macroscopic quantum phenomena. A double Fock state—two condensates each prepared with a fixed, well-defined particle number—represents an extreme case of phase indeterminacy: by number-phase uncertainty, the relative phase between the two condensates is maximally undefined at the outset. Yet numerous theoretical and experimental studies have shown that a sequence of measurements performed on individual atoms extracted from such a state can cause an apparent relative phase to emerge dynamically, even though no phase was present in the initial global wavefunction. This work provides a detailed theoretical analysis of this phenomenon using the formalism of collective transverse spin measurements, treating the two-mode Bose gas as a large effective spin system and tracking the conditional quantum state as successive single-particle measurements are performed.

## Model and Method

We consider $N$ bosonic atoms distributed between two modes—which may represent two spatially separated condensates, two hyperfine states, or two arms of an atomic interferometer—prepared initially in a Fock state with equal or well-defined populations in each mode, $|N/2, N/2\rangle$. This state can be mapped onto a large collective pseudo-spin of length $N/2$, polarized along the $z$-axis, with $S_z$ eigenvalue fixed and complete uncertainty in the transverse spin components $S_x$ and $S_y$—directly reflecting the absence of a defined relative phase.

To probe the emergence of phase, we simulate a protocol in which single particles are extracted one at a time from the combined system and subjected to a measurement in the transverse spin basis, equivalent to interfering the particle with itself in a beam-splitter type setup and measuring its output port. Each single-particle measurement outcome provides partial information about the collective transverse spin orientation of the remaining $N-1$ particles, and via Bayesian-like backaction, incrementally projects the many-body state closer to a spin-coherent state polarized in some particular direction in the $x$–$y$ plane. This method allows us to construct, step by step, the conditional quantum state of the atomic ensemble as a function of the number of measurements performed, $m$, and to compute observables and higher-order correlation functions—including quantities suitable for testing Bell-type inequalities—at each stage of the measurement sequence.

## Rapid Emergence of a Quasi-Classical Phase

Our central finding is that the collective quantum state converges extremely rapidly toward a quasi-classical description characterized by a well-defined relative phase. Already after a number of measurements $m$ that is small compared to the total particle number $N$, the conditional state of the unmeasured atoms becomes very close to a spin-coherent state: the transverse spin components acquire a definite mean value and reduced fluctuations, and successive single-particle measurement outcomes become highly correlated, exhibiting near-perfect alignment of individual spins along a common (yet randomly selected, shot-to-shot) direction in the transverse plane. This behavior reproduces, from a fully quantum many-body treatment, the intuitive picture in which a "spontaneous" phase appears between the two condensates as a result of the measurement process itself, mimicking what one would expect from two condensates that possessed a genuine relative phase from the outset. Correlation functions between spins computed in this regime closely match the predictions of local hidden-variable or classical probabilistic models, and the degree of polarization of the effective spin approaches unity extremely fast, scaling favorably with $N$, thereby explaining why experiments with large atom numbers typically observe an almost instantaneously well-defined interference pattern.

## Reemergence of Quantum Correlations Near Full Depletion

The picture changes qualitatively, however, when the number of measurements $m$ approaches the total particle number $N$. As the reservoir of unmeasured particles is depleted, the remaining atoms constitute an increasingly small quantum system, and the conditional state can no longer be approximated by a classical, macroscopically-populated coherent spin state. In this regime, we find that genuinely quantum correlations reemerge in the statistics of the measurement outcomes. Specifically, by constructing appropriate correlation functions among the last few measured spins—analogous to those used in Clauser-Horne-Shimony-Holt (CHSH)-type Bell tests—we demonstrate that the resulting inequality violations can become as large as those obtained in the canonical case of just two entangled spin-1/2 particles. This is a striking result: despite the fact that the system started as a large many-body ensemble of $N$ particles and underwent a long sequence of measurements that drove it toward apparently classical behavior, the last few atoms to be measured retain—or dynamically regenerate—a degree of quantum entanglement and nonlocal correlation on par with the maximally entangled two-particle case.

## Discussion and Implications

These results illuminate a subtle interplay between the size of a quantum system and the robustness of its quantum-to-classical transition under sequential measurement. While the majority of the measurement sequence follows a rapid, exponential-like convergence toward classical, quasi-coherent behavior—consistent with expectations from decoherence and the emergence of "spontaneous" symmetry breaking of phase in the thermodynamic limit—the terminal measurements, performed on a vanishingly small remaining subsystem, expose the underlying quantum entanglement structure of the original Fock state. This demonstrates that the appearance of classicality in large Bose-Einstein condensate systems is a residual, emergent phenomenon rather than a fundamental property of the state itself, and that quantum nonlocality of Bell-inequality-violating strength persists at the microscopic core of the many-body wavefunction even after most of the system has been measured. The persistence of such strong nonlocal correlations, comparable to the elementary two-qubit case, underscores the resilience of quantum coherence in many-body systems and suggests new avenues for probing entanglement structure in large ensembles through carefully designed sequential or adaptive measurement schemes. More broadly, this work contributes to the understanding of how classicality emerges dynamically from measurement in large quantum systems, and it highlights that the correspondence between many-body quantum mechanics and effective classical descriptions, though extremely robust in bulk, can break down sharply when a system is probed down to its last few constituent quanta.

# Bose, Einstein, and Fock: Foundations of Quantum Statistics

The names Bose, Einstein, and Fock are inextricably linked to some of the most fundamental developments in quantum statistical mechanics and quantum field theory, shaping our understanding of how identical particles behave in the quantum realm.

## Bose and the Birth of Quantum Statistics

In 1924, the Indian physicist Satyendra Nath Bose made a groundbreaking contribution to physics when he derived Planck's law of blackbody radiation using a novel statistical approach. Rather than treating photons as distinguishable particles following classical statistics, Bose proposed treating them as indistinguishable entities, counting the number of ways photons could be distributed among energy states without regard to which specific photon occupied which state. This seemingly simple conceptual shift proved revolutionary, as it resolved inconsistencies in the classical treatment of radiation.

## Einstein's Extension

Bose sent his paper to Albert Einstein, who immediately recognized its significance. Einstein not only helped get the paper published but extended Bose's statistical method to material particles with mass, predicting that at sufficiently low temperatures, particles obeying these statistics would condense into the lowest available quantum state—a phenomenon now known as Bose-Einstein condensation. This prediction, made in 1924-1925, was not experimentally confirmed until 1995, when physicists Eric Cornell and Carl Wieman successfully created the first Bose-Einstein condensate using rubidium atoms cooled to nanokelvin temperatures, work that earned them the Nobel Prize in Physics in 2001.

The statistical framework they developed—now called Bose-Einstein statistics—applies to particles known as bosons, which include photons, gluons, and other force-carrying particles, as well as composite particles like certain atoms. Unlike fermions, which obey the Pauli exclusion principle, bosons can occupy the same quantum state simultaneously, a property that underlies phenomena ranging from laser light to superconductivity.

## Fock's Mathematical Formalism

Building on these foundational insights, the Soviet physicist Vladimir Fock introduced crucial mathematical machinery in 1932 that would become indispensable to quantum field theory. Fock developed what is now known as Fock space—a mathematical construction that elegantly handles systems with variable or unknown particle numbers. This is essential in quantum field theory, where particles can be created and destroyed.

Fock space is built from a direct sum of tensor products of single-particle Hilbert spaces, appropriately symmetrized or antisymmetrized depending on whether the particles are bosons or fermions. This formalism introduced creation and annihilation operators, which add or remove particles from a given quantum state, providing the mathematical language necessary to describe processes like photon emission and absorption, particle-antiparticle pair production, and other fundamental interactions in quantum electrodynamics and beyond.

## A Unified Legacy

Together, the contributions of Bose, Einstein, and Fock form a coherent intellectual lineage: Bose's statistical insight for photons, Einstein's generalization to massive particles, and Fock's rigorous mathematical framework for handling variable particle numbers collectively established the theoretical bedrock upon which modern quantum field theory and condensed matter physics are built. Their combined legacy continues to inform cutting-edge research, from ultracold atom experiments to the theoretical underpinnings of the Standard Model of particle physics.

# Emergence of Relative Phase Between Two Bose-Einstein Condensates via Sequential Measurements of Transverse Spin

## Abstract

We investigate the dynamical emergence of a well-defined relative phase between two initially independent Bose-Einstein condensates through repeated, weak measurements of collective transverse spin operators, extending the pioneering analysis of Javanainen and Yoo to a fully sequential measurement framework. While a single measurement of the relative atom number or a single interference snapshot is known to project the combined many-body state onto a state exhibiting phase coherence despite the absence of any pre-existing individual condensate phases, the robustness and dynamics of this phase-locking under a continuous stream of measurements has remained an open question central to understanding the quantum-to-classical transition of matter-wave coherence. Here we model the process as a sequence of weak, generalized measurements of the collective pseudo-spin components $\hat{J}_x$ and $\hat{J}_y$, formed from atomic operators of the two condensate modes, and derive the resulting stochastic master equation governing the conditional quantum state. We show that successive measurement outcomes progressively narrow the distribution of the inferred relative phase, driving the system toward a phase eigenstate at a rate set by the measurement strength and the total atom number, while simultaneously inducing measurement back-action that broadens the conjugate relative-number distribution consistent with the Heisenberg uncertainty relation. Numerical simulations of the quantum trajectories reveal that the phase diffusion coefficient scales inversely with the square of the atom number, indicating that macroscopic condensates rapidly acquire an emergent, measurement-induced classical phase difference even when no such phase existed in the initial product Fock state. We further demonstrate that the statistics of the accumulated measurement record reproduce the interference fringe visibility and phase distribution predicted by single-shot matter-wave interferometry experiments, thereby providing a continuous-measurement derivation and generalization of these established results. Our findings clarify the physical origin of spontaneously interfering condensates as a genuine measurement-induced symmetry-breaking phenomenon, offer a quantitative framework for the buildup of coherence under realistic, non-instantaneous detection protocols, and suggest that engineered sequential-measurement schemes could be used to actively steer and stabilize the relative phase in coupled atomic condensates for applications in precision interferometry and quantum metrology.

# Repeated Transverse Spin Measurements on Double Fock States: From Emergent Classicality to Bell Violations

This is a fascinating topic connecting quantum measurement theory, spontaneous symmetry breaking, and quantum information. Let me walk through the physics systematically.

## 1. The Initial State: Double Fock State

Consider two modes (e.g., two spatial wells, or two internal atomic states) each containing definite particle number, forming a **double Fock state**:
$$|\psi\rangle = |N_a, N_b\rangle$$

Key feature: this state has **no definite relative phase**. In the Schwinger boson representation, treating the two modes as a collective spin:
$$\hat{J}_z = \frac{1}{2}(\hat{a}^\dagger\hat{a} - \hat{b}^\dagger\hat{b}), \quad \hat{J}_x, \hat{J}_y \text{ (transverse spins)}$$

The Fock state is an eigenstate of $\hat{J}_z$ with **zero variance in population difference**, but by the number-phase uncertainty relation, the relative phase $\phi$ is **maximally uncertain** — uniformly distributed over $[0, 2\pi)$. This is fundamentally different from a coherent spin state (which has a well-defined phase from the start).

## 2. Single Transverse Spin Measurement

A transverse spin measurement (e.g., measuring $\hat{J}_\theta = \hat{J}_x\cos\theta + \hat{J}_y\sin\theta$) is implemented by:
- Applying a beam-splitter-like pulse (a $\pi/2$ rotation) mixing the two modes
- Detecting the number of atoms in each output port

For a single pair of atoms drawn from the condensate, measuring $\hat{J}_\theta$ projects onto eigenstates that are **coherent superpositions** of $|N_a,N_b\rangle$ components — effectively probing "which phase" information indirectly.

Crucially, a **single measurement outcome is random** — it doesn't reveal a pre-existing phase, because none exists in the Fock state. The measurement *creates* correlations rather than reading out a hidden variable.

## 3. Emergence of Classical Phase via Repeated Measurements

The key physics (studied by Castin, Dalibard, Javanainen, Mølmer and others) is:

**Single measurement**: A single transverse spin measurement on a genuine double Fock state gives an outcome, but the *conditional state* of the remaining atoms becomes progressively less uncertain in phase.

**Sequential measurement scheme**: Suppose we don't measure all atoms simultaneously, but perform a **sequence of weak measurements** on small subsets of the atoms (or repeatedly measure transverse spin projections and use Bayesian updating on the many-body state):

1. Each measurement outcome $J_\theta^{(k)}$ depends on both $\theta_k$ and the (initially undefined) phase $\phi$.
2. After the first measurement, the conditional quantum state of the remaining $N-1$ (or $N-2$) atoms is **no longer phase-symmetric** — it becomes a superposition sharply peaked around some phase value $\phi_0$, consistent with the observed outcome.
3. Subsequent measurements are then very likely to yield outcomes **consistent with this same $\phi_0$**, sharpening the phase distribution further (a self-consistent Bayesian narrowing, analogous to the emergence of a "classical" pointer state).

Mathematically, the projected state after $M$ measurements behaves like:
$$|\psi_M\rangle \sim \int d\phi \, e^{-M(\phi - \phi_0)^2/2\sigma^2} |\phi\rangle$$

where $|\phi\rangle$ is the phase (coherent spin) state $\propto (\hat{a}^\dagger + e^{i\phi}\hat{b}^\dagger)^N|0\rangle$. As $M$ grows, this Gaussian narrows, and the ensemble of atoms **behaves as though it had a definite relative phase from the start** — despite the initial state having none. This is the hallmark of **spontaneous symmetry breaking under repeated (weak) measurement**: the phase is not pre-existing but is *dynamically selected* by the measurement process itself, with the specific value $\phi_0$ being random from shot to shot (matching the original $U(1)$ symmetry of the Fock state on average over many experimental realizations).

This is directly analogous to how a series of weak position measurements can localize a delocalized wavefunction, or how measuring $\sigma_z$ repeatedly on subsystems of a large spin can "decohere" superpositions into apparent classical outcomes.

## 4. Connection to Bell Inequality Violations

Here's where it becomes genuinely quantum-informationally interesting:

### (a) Two spatially separated condensates
Consider the double Fock state distributed between two **spatially separated modes** (e.g., two wells $A$ and $B$, each further split so Alice holds part of $A$'s atoms and Bob holds part of $B$'s). The **number-conserving entanglement** in the original Fock state is highly nonclassical: it's an entangled state of the form (schematically) $\sum_n c_n |n\rangle_A|N-n\rangle_B$.

### (b) Local transverse spin measurements = local Bell-test observables
Alice and Bob each perform local transverse spin measurements (choosing measurement angles $\theta_A, \theta_B$) — analogous to choosing polarizer angles in photonic Bell tests. The dichotomic outcomes (sign of local population difference, or which output port fires) serve as the $\pm 1$ outcomes for a **CHSH-type inequality**:
$$S = E(\theta_A,\theta_B) - E(\theta_A,\theta_B') + E(\theta_A',\theta_B) + E(\theta_A',\theta_B')$$

### (c) Why repeated measurement matters
For **small atom number** or single-pair measurements, the number-conserving entangled state can directly violate Bell/CHSH inequalities (as shown theoretically e.g. by Gross, Oudot, or the "atomic homodyne" proposals of He, Reid, Drummond). But:

- For **many atoms measured collectively** (as in typical BEC experiments), if a *single* collective transverse spin measurement is used, the correlations tend to look classical (Gaussian, consistent with local hidden phase variables) because of the emergent phase-locking described above — the system behaves like it has a classical phase $\phi$ shared by both sides, mimicking a local hidden variable model.
- However, when one examines **higher-order correlations** — i.e., correlations between **repeated/sequential** measurement outcomes, or measures **beyond mean-field fluctuations** (looking at the full counting statistics, not just averages) — the quantum correlations from number entanglement re-emerge and violate a Bell/CHSH-type inequality **despite the apparent classical phase**.

This subtlety is the crux of theoretical work (e.g., by Sørensen, Duan, Cirac, Zoller on spin squeezing; and by He, Reid, Drummond, and separately Laloë & Mullin on Bell tests with number-conserving BEC states): the emergent classical phase governs *first-moment* (mean-field) behavior, but the **quantum correlations violating Bell inequalities live in the higher-order (fluctuation) statistics** that survive the "symmetry-broken" phase-locked description. Essentially:

$$\text{Local phase emerges} \;\Longrightarrow\; \text{classical-looking mean-field} $$
$$\text{But full counting statistics} \;\Longrightarrow\; \text{genuine entanglement} \Longrightarrow \text{Bell violation}$$

## Summary Picture

| Stage | Physical Picture |
|---|---|
| Initial state | Double Fock state: no phase, maximal number entanglement between modes |
| Single/weak transverse spin measurements | Random outcome, projects conditional state toward a phase value |
| Repeated measurements | Bayesian narrowing → emergent, apparently "classical," well-defined relative phase (symmetry breaking by measurement) |
| Spatial separation + local measurements | Setup becomes formally analogous to EPR/Bell scenario |
| Analysis of full correlations (not just mean-field) | Residual quantum correlations from original number entanglement produce CHSH/Bell inequality violations, revealing that the emergent "classical" phase is not a true local hidden variable |

The overall lesson is that **measurement-induced classicality (phase emergence) and genuine quantum nonlocality are not mutually exclusive** — the double Fock state's entanglement is robust enough that, properly analyzed through repeated/local measurement statistics, it can still expose Bell-inequality-violating correlations, even though a naïve mean-field/single-shot analysis would suggest the system has "collapsed" onto a classical phase reference.

# Measurement-Induced Phase Emergence in Bosonic Double Fock States

## Overview

This line of theoretical research examines how definite relative phases can spontaneously emerge from measurements performed on double Fock states—superpositions of two modes each containing a well-defined number of bosons (atoms or photons), where no phase relationship is initially specified. This connects to fundamental questions about the quantum-to-classical transition and the persistence of nonlocal correlations as particle number increases.

## Key Concepts

**Double Fock States**: These states, of the form |N,N⟩ (N particles in each of two modes), possess a U(1) gauge symmetry—no definite phase exists between the modes before measurement. This differs from coherent states, which have a pre-defined phase but indefinite particle number.

**Phase Emergence via Measurement**: When quadrature-type (homodyne-like) measurements are performed on such states, a well-defined relative phase can emerge dynamically as a product of the measurement process itself, rather than being present in the initial state. This is analogous to spontaneous symmetry breaking, but induced by measurement back-action rather than by interactions or environmental decoherence.

## Connection to CHSH Inequality

The central finding connects this phase emergence to tests of quantum nonlocality:

- **Bell-type correlations** can be constructed using spin-like operators derived from the double Fock states after appropriate homodyne measurements induce relative phase information.
- The **CHSH (Clauser-Horne-Shimony-Holt) inequality**, a specific formulation of Bell's inequality involving correlation functions measured at different settings, can be violated using these mesoscopic states.
- Crucially, violations were shown to **persist for large N** (large particle numbers), counter to naive expectations that quantum nonlocality should be washed out or become experimentally inaccessible as systems become macroscopic.

## Significance

1. **Macroscopic Quantum Nonlocality**: The results suggest that entanglement and Bell-inequality violations are not inherently restricted to microscopic systems; with appropriate measurement schemes, they can survive scaling to many-particle regimes.

2. **Role of Measurement in Symmetry Breaking**: The work illustrates a conceptually important mechanism where measurement acts as the agent generating an effectively classical parameter (phase) from a symmetric quantum state, offering insight into decoherence and classicalization processes distinct from environmental interaction.

3. **Experimental Relevance**: These theoretical predictions are directly relevant to experiments with ultracold atoms (e.g., Bose-Einstein condensates split into two wells) and quantum optics setups (twin photon beams), where double Fock states can be prepared and homodyne-type measurements are experimentally accessible.

## Caveat

This is a summary reconstructed based on the described theoretical framework; if you are referencing a specific paper (e.g., by a particular author or in a particular journal), let me know so I can tailor details—such as specific mathematical results, named operators, or particular authors' models—more precisely.

# Abstract

We investigate the role of continuous quantum measurement in the emergence of classical behavior from spin correlations in two-mode Bose-Einstein condensates (BECs). Two-mode BECs, described by collective pseudo-spin operators satisfying SU(2) algebra, exhibit a rich interplay between unitary many-body dynamics and measurement-induced decoherence. We show that weak, continuous measurement of the relative phase between the condensate modes drives a dynamical instability analogous to spontaneous symmetry breaking: an initially symmetric, phase-undefined many-body state evolves stochastically toward states of well-defined relative phase, effectively selecting a classical symmetry-broken configuration from the underlying U(1) invariance of the Hamiltonian. This measurement-induced localization occurs on a timescale that scales favorably with the total atom number N, becoming increasingly sharp and deterministic in the large-N limit, consistent with the expected quantum-to-classical crossover.

Surprisingly, we find that despite this apparent loss of coherence at the level of the reduced single-particle description, genuine quantum correlations among the constituent spins are not destroyed but instead re-emerge and become more pronounced as N grows. Using measures of entanglement and quantum discord conditioned on the measurement record, we demonstrate that the stochastic trajectories generate strong multipartite correlations that persist even as the mean-field (semiclassical) relative phase stabilizes. We trace this counterintuitive behavior to the structure of the measurement backaction, which locally projects the collective spin while simultaneously entangling the internal constituents through the nonlinear coupling inherent to the two-mode Hamiltonian. Our results reconcile the emergence of classical, symmetry-broken order parameters with the persistence and amplification of quantum correlations in mesoscopic and macroscopic spin ensembles, offering insight into the general mechanism by which measurement can simultaneously classicalize collective observables while generating or preserving genuine quantum resources at the microscopic level. These findings have implications for quantum metrology, entanglement generation in cold-atom platforms, and the broader theory of measurement-induced phase transitions in many-body quantum systems.

# Abstract

We investigate the entanglement properties of double Fock states in Bose-Einstein condensates (BECs) through the lens of transverse pseudo-spin measurements performed on two spatially separated modes. Starting from a twin-Fock state with N atoms equally distributed between two condensate modes, we construct collective transverse spin operators analogous to those used in discrete-variable spin-1/2 Bell tests. By introducing local phase references (phase-locking) between the beam splitters used to recombine and measure atoms from each mode, we show that correlations between transverse spin projections can be measured with high fidelity despite the intrinsically bosonic and multi-particle nature of the double Fock state.

We derive the correlation functions for transverse spin measurements as a function of the relative phases and mode populations, and construct a Bell-CHSH-type inequality using four judiciously chosen phase settings. Our analysis demonstrates that despite the large particle number, the correlations violate the CHSH bound in a manner structurally identical to the elementary two-spin (EPR-Bohm) case, achieving comparable violation strengths of up to $2\sqrt{2}$ in the ideal limit. This result establishes that mesoscopic atomic double Fock states preserve genuine multipartite-like nonlocal correlations under phase-locked homodyne-type detection, reducible to an effective two-outcome, two-setting scenario. We discuss the role of phase diffusion, finite detection efficiency, and particle loss in degrading the violation, and identify realistic experimental regimes—accessible with current cold-atom interferometry techniques—capable of demonstrating this violation. These findings extend Bell-type nonlocality tests to genuinely many-body bosonic systems and open pathways toward loophole-resistant tests of quantum mechanics using ultracold atomic ensembles.
